claim: SerpinE2 and HtrA1 modulate fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling in germ layer specification and head-to-tail development of Xenopus embryos.
source: We previously showed that SerpinE2 and the serine protease HtrA1 modulate fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signaling in germ layer specification and head-to-tail development of Xenopus embryos.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Knockdown of SerpinE2 by injected antisense morpholino oligonucleotides did not affect the specification of NC progenitors.
source: Knockdown of SerpinE2 by injected antisense morpholino oligonucleotides did not affect the specification of NC progenitors but instead inhibited the migration of NC cells, causing defects in dorsal fin, melanocyte, and craniofacial cartilage formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Knockdown of SerpinE2 inhibited the migration of NC cells, causing defects in dorsal fin, melanocyte, and craniofacial cartilage formation.
source: Knockdown of SerpinE2 by injected antisense morpholino oligonucleotides did not affect the specification of NC progenitors but instead inhibited the migration of NC cells, causing defects in dorsal fin, melanocyte, and craniofacial cartilage formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments and phenotypic analysis.

claim: Overexpression of the HtrA1 protease impaired NC cell migration and the formation of NC-derived structures.
source: Similarly, overexpression of the HtrA1 protease impaired NC cell migration and the formation of NC-derived structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mRNA overexpression experiments.

claim: The phenotype of SerpinE2 knockdown was overcome by concomitant downregulation of HtrA1.
source: The phenotype of SerpinE2 knockdown was overcome by concomitant downregulation of HtrA1, indicating that SerpinE2 stimulates NC migration by inhibiting endogenous HtrA1 activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by epistatic experimental data from double knockdown experiments.

claim: SerpinE2 stimulates NC migration by inhibiting endogenous HtrA1 activity.
source: The phenotype of SerpinE2 knockdown was overcome by concomitant downregulation of HtrA1, indicating that SerpinE2 stimulates NC migration by inhibiting endogenous HtrA1 activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the epistatic experimental results showing rescue of phenotype.

claim: SerpinE2 binds to HtrA1.
source: SerpinE2 binds to HtrA1, and the HtrA1 protease triggers degradation of the cell surface proteoglycan Syndecan-4 (Sdc4).
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical binding data referenced from previous work.

claim: The HtrA1 protease triggers degradation of the cell surface proteoglycan Syndecan-4 (Sdc4).
source: SerpinE2 binds to HtrA1, and the HtrA1 protease triggers degradation of the cell surface proteoglycan Syndecan-4 (Sdc4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from previous work and current study.

claim: Microinjection of Sdc4 mRNA partially rescued NC migration defects induced by HtrA1 upregulation.
source: Microinjection of Sdc4 mRNA partially rescued NC migration defects induced by both HtrA1 upregulation and SerpinE2 downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rescue experiments.

claim: Microinjection of Sdc4 mRNA partially rescued NC migration defects induced by SerpinE2 downregulation.
source: Microinjection of Sdc4 mRNA partially rescued NC migration defects induced by both HtrA1 upregulation and SerpinE2 downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rescue experiments.

claim: SerpinE2, HtrA1, and Syndecan-4 form a proteolytic pathway regulating NC cell migration through a double inhibition mechanism.
source: These epistatic experiments suggest a proteolytic pathway by a double inhibition mechanism:SerpinE2 ┤HtrA1 protease ┤Syndecan-4 → NC cell migration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of epistatic experiments.

claim: Collective cell migration is a fundamental process in the development and maintenance of multicellular organisms.
source: Collective cell migration is a fundamental process in the development and maintenance of multicellular organisms (Friedl and Gilmour, 2009; Shellard and Mayor, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Aberrant cell migration is linked to cancer metastasis.
source: Embryonic development relies on the coordinated movement of cells to specific locations, and aberrant cell migration is linked to cancer metastasis.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The acquisition of cell motility is associated with an epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT).
source: The acquisition of cell motility is associated with an epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), in which cells disrupt epithelial adhesions and remodel junctional complexes in favor of cell-matrix adhesions to adopt a migratory behavior (Nieto et al., 2016; Piacentino et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The neural crest (NC) is a multipotent cell population that is specified at the border of the neural plate.
source: The NC is a multipotent cell population that is specified at the border of the neural plate (Le Douarin and Kalcheim, 1999; Schock et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: EMT initiates migration streams of NC cells toward their targets where they differentiate into diverse cell types and tissues, including peripheral nervous system, melanocytes, and craniofacial skeleton.
source: EMT initiates migration streams of NC cells toward their targets where they differentiate into diverse cell types and tissues, including peripheral nervous system, melanocytes, and craniofacial skeleton.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about neural crest development.

claim: The behavior of NC cells recapitulates certain stages of cancer progression and metastasis.
source: The behavior of NC cells recapitulates certain stages of cancer progression and metastasis (Nieto et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Defects in NC development can lead to many congenital syndromes and tumors of the NC lineage.
source: Defects in NC development can lead to many congenital syndromes and tumors of the NC lineage (Medina-Cuadra and Monsoro-Burq, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: HtrA1 belongs to a conserved family of serine proteases that are homologous to the heat shock-induced HtrA peptidase from bacteria.
source: HtrA1 belongs to a conserved family of serine proteases that are homologous to the heat shock-induced HtrA (high temperature requirement A) peptidase from bacteria and primarily involved in protein quality control and degradation (Zurawa-Janicka et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Vertebrate HtrA proteases comprise four members HtrA1–4.
source: Vertebrate HtrA proteases, comprising the four members HtrA1–4, share a trypsin serine protease domain and a carboxyterminal PDZ domain with their bacterial counterpart.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Vertebrate HtrA proteases share a trypsin serine protease domain and a carboxyterminal PDZ domain with their bacterial counterpart.
source: Vertebrate HtrA proteases, comprising the four members HtrA1–4, share a trypsin serine protease domain and a carboxyterminal PDZ domain with their bacterial counterpart.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The HtrA family is implicated in various pathological conditions including cancer, arthritis, neurodegenerative diseases, and pregnancy disorders.
source: The HtrA family is implicated in various pathological conditions including cancer, arthritis, neurodegenerative diseases, and pregnancy disorders.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: HtrA1 modulates the extracellular matrix and cell signaling as a secreted protein.
source: HtrA1 modulates the extracellular matrix and cell signaling as a secreted protein but was found to be active in the cytoplasm and nucleus, too (Clawson et al., 2008; Chien et al., 2009a; Campioni et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: HtrA1 was found to be active in the cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: HtrA1 modulates the extracellular matrix and cell signaling as a secreted protein but was found to be active in the cytoplasm and nucleus, too (Clawson et al., 2008; Chien et al., 2009a; Campioni et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The function of HtrA1 in cell migration has been studied in vitro to reveal mainly a negative role, although also a positive role has been reported.
source: The function of HtrA1 in cell migration has been studied in vitro to reveal mainly a negative role, although also a positive role has been reported (Pei et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: How HtrA1 activities are regulated is poorly understood.
source: How HtrA1 activities are regulated is poorly understood, and the mechanism by which this protease affects cell migration in vivo remains elusive.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The mechanism by which HtrA1 affects cell migration in vivo remains elusive.
source: How HtrA1 activities are regulated is poorly understood, and the mechanism by which this protease affects cell migration in vivo remains elusive.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Members of the serpin superfamily contain a carboxyterminal reactive center loop (RCL) that covalently binds to and inhibits target serine proteases inside and outside of cells.
source: Members of the serpin superfamily contain a carboxyterminal reactive center loop (RCL) that covalently binds to and inhibits target serine proteases inside and outside of cells (Olson and Gettins, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: SerpinE2 has important roles in the nervous, blood, and reproductive systems.
source: Serpin peptidase inhibitor clade E member 2 (SerpinE2), also known as protease nexin-1 (PN1) or glia-derived nexin, has important roles in the nervous, blood, and reproductive systems (Arocas and Bouton, 2015; Monard, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: SerpinE2 functions as a key factor in tumor dissemination.
source: SerpinE2 also functions as a key factor in tumor dissemination, but the molecular mechanism by which this protease inhibitor governs cell migration and metastasis is largely unknown.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The molecular mechanism by which SerpinE2 governs cell migration and metastasis is largely unknown.
source: SerpinE2 also functions as a key factor in tumor dissemination, but the molecular mechanism by which this protease inhibitor governs cell migration and metastasis is largely unknown.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: HtrA1 and SerpinE2 are transcriptionally induced by fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signals.
source: We previously showed that HtrA1 and SerpinE2 are transcriptionally induced by fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signals and act as feedback regulators of FGF/Erk signaling in germ layer and anteroposterior axis formation in the early Xenopus embryo (Hou et al., 2007; Acosta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: HtrA1 and SerpinE2 act as feedback regulators of FGF/Erk signaling in germ layer and anteroposterior axis formation in the early Xenopus embryo.
source: We previously showed that HtrA1 and SerpinE2 are transcriptionally induced by fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signals and act as feedback regulators of FGF/Erk signaling in germ layer and anteroposterior axis formation in the early Xenopus embryo (Hou et al., 2007; Acosta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: HtrA1 activates Erk and expression of the transcription factor Brachyury in the posterior mesoderm.
source: HtrA1 activates Erk (extracellular signal-regulated kinase) and expression of the transcription factor Brachyury in the posterior mesoderm, whereas SerpinE2 suppresses Erk activation and Brachyury expression in the anterior ectoderm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: SerpinE2 suppresses Erk activation and Brachyury expression in the anterior ectoderm.
source: HtrA1 activates Erk (extracellular signal-regulated kinase) and expression of the transcription factor Brachyury in the posterior mesoderm, whereas SerpinE2 suppresses Erk activation and Brachyury expression in the anterior ectoderm.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: The HtrA1 protease releases FGF ligands by triggering the cleavage of cell surface proteoglycans such as Syndecan-4 (Sdc4), thereby stimulating FGF/Erk signaling in mesoderm and trunk/tail formation.
source: The HtrA1 protease releases FGF ligands by triggering the cleavage of cell surface proteoglycans such as Syndecan-4 (Sdc4), thereby stimulating FGF/Erk signaling in mesoderm and trunk/tail formation (Hou et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: SerpinE2 binds to and inhibits HtrA1, thus restricting FGF/Erk signaling and allowing ectoderm and head formation to occur.
source: SerpinE2 binds to and inhibits HtrA1, thus restricting FGF/Erk signaling and allowing ectoderm and head formation to occur (Acosta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: SerpinE2 and HtrA1 exhibit overlapping gene expression in the NC.
source: Since SerpinE2 and HtrA1 exhibit overlapping gene expression in the NC, we now asked whether these proteins might have a role in NC development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from in situ hybridization shown in the manuscript.

claim: At neurula stage 17, Twist expression labeled pre-migratory NC cells in the deep layer of the ectoderm.
source: At neurula stage 17, Twist expression labeled pre-migratory NC cells in the deep layer of the ectoderm (Figure 1A and A'; Hopwood et al., 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1 and cited literature.

claim: SerpinE2 transcripts were found in the deep layer of the neural plate and adjacent NC cells at stage 17.
source: SerpinE2 transcripts were found in the deep layer of the neural plate and adjacent NC cells (Figure 1B and B').
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: HtrA1 was transcribed in the superficial layer of the neural plate and in the NC at stage 17.
source: HtrA1 was transcribed in the superficial layer of the neural plate and in the NC (Figure 1C and C').
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: At stage 26, SerpinE2 and HtrA1 were co-expressed with Twist in ventrally migrating NC cells in the mandibular, hyoid, anterior branchial, and posterior branchial streams.
source: At stage 26, SerpinE2 and HtrA1 were co-expressed with Twist in ventrally migrating NC cells in the mandibular, hyoid, anterior branchial, and posterior branchial streams (numbered as 1–4 in Figure 1D–F; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: SerpinE2 transcripts accumulated at the ventral leading front of migrating NC cohorts at stage 26.
source: Importantly, SerpinE2 transcripts accumulated at the ventral leading front, while HtrA1 expression was abundant in more dorsal follower cells within the migrating NC cohorts (Figure 1D'–F'; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: HtrA1 expression was abundant in more dorsal follower cells within the migrating NC cohorts at stage 26.
source: Importantly, SerpinE2 transcripts accumulated at the ventral leading front, while HtrA1 expression was abundant in more dorsal follower cells within the migrating NC cohorts (Figure 1D'–F'; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: SerpinE2 and HtrA1 shared overlapping expression in the brain, eye vesicles, and otic placodes at stage 26.
source: In addition, SerpinE2 and HtrA1 shared overlapping expression in the brain, eye vesicles, and otic placodes (Figure 1E and F; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Bilateral removal of the neural folds in the cranial and anterior trunk region of a mid-neurula embryo at stage 17 resulted in larvae displaying a reduced head size, missing dorsal fin, and reduced melanocyte pigmentation.
source: We reproduced these findings in Xenopus and showed that bilateral removal of the neural folds (anlagen of the NC) in the cranial and anterior trunk region of a mid-neurula embryo at stage 17 resulted in larvae displaying a reduced head size, missing dorsal fin (open arrowheads), and reduced melanocyte pigmentation (arrow) (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from neural crest extirpation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Microinjection of SerpinE2-MO at doses of 40 ng per embryo caused a reduction of head tissue, dorsal fin structures, and melanocytes at stage 40.
source: A closer analysis now revealed that these SerpinE2-morphant embryos also exhibited a loss of dorsal fin structures (open arrowheads) and a decreased number of melanocytes (arrow) at stage 40 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: A standard control-MO had no phenotypic effect on embryo development.
source: These phenotypes were specific, since a standard control-MO had no phenotypic effect (Figure 2D), and co-injection of SerpinE2-MO together with a Flag-SerpinE2 mRNA that is not targeted by the MO rescued normal development (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from control experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Co-injection of SerpinE2-MO together with a Flag-SerpinE2 mRNA that is not targeted by the MO rescued normal development.
source: These phenotypes were specific, since a standard control-MO had no phenotypic effect (Figure 2D), and co-injection of SerpinE2-MO together with a Flag-SerpinE2 mRNA that is not targeted by the MO rescued normal development (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: SerpinE2-MO does not affect NC specification in the head and trunk, as the expression of Twist, Sox9, cMyc, Foxd3, Snail1, and Snail2 in pre-migratory NC cells remained unchanged in mid-neurula embryos at stage 18.
source: SerpinE2-MO does not appear to affect NC specification in the head and trunk, as the expression of Twist, Sox9, cMyc, Foxd3, Snail1, and Snail2 in pre-migratory NC cells remained unchanged in mid-neurula embryos at stage 18 (Figure 2H–K; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2.

claim: A single dorsal injection of SerpinE2-MO caused a delay or failure of NC cells to undergo EMT and migration in advanced neurula and tailbud embryos.
source: A single dorsal injection of SerpinE2-MO caused a delay or failure of these NC cells to undergo EMT and migration (open arrowheads) in advanced neurula (Figure 2M and P) and tailbud embryos (Figure 2S).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: A SerpinE2-5MM-MO, which contains five mismatches with the SerpinE2.L and SerpinE2.S target mRNA sequences, failed to disrupt NC migration.
source: These knockdown effects were specific, because a SerpinE2-5MM-MO, which contains five mismatches with the SerpinE2.L and SerpinE2.S target mRNA sequences, as well as a combination of SerpinE2-MO and non-targeted Flag-SerpinE2 mRNA failed to disrupt NC migration (Figure 2N, Q, and T; see also Figure 8B–E' and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from control experiments shown in Figure 2 and Figure 8.

claim: A combination of SerpinE2-MO and non-targeted Flag-SerpinE2 mRNA failed to disrupt NC migration.
source: These knockdown effects were specific, because a SerpinE2-5MM-MO, which contains five mismatches with the SerpinE2.L and SerpinE2.S target mRNA sequences, as well as a combination of SerpinE2-MO and non-targeted Flag-SerpinE2 mRNA failed to disrupt NC migration (Figure 2N, Q, and T; see also Figure 8B–E' and Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 2 and Figure 8.

claim: Ventrally injected SerpinE2-MO was less efficient in reducing NC migration because expression of SerpinE2 is highest in dorsal regions of post-gastrula embryos.
source: Ventrally injected SerpinE2-MO was less efficient in reducing NC migration (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C and D), because expression of the SerpinE2 is highest in dorsal regions of post-gastrula embryos (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and expression pattern.

claim: SerpinE2 is dispensable for the initial specification but necessary for the migration of NC cells in Xenopus embryos.
source: We conclude that SerpinE2 is dispensable for the initial specification but necessary for the migration of NC cells in Xenopus embryos.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results.

claim: Injection of HtrA1 mRNA into the animal pole blastomeres led to a decrease of head and eye structures in early tadpole embryos.
source: Injection of HtrA1 mRNA into the animal pole blastomeres led to a decrease of head and eye structures in early tadpole embryos (Figure 3A and B) in accordance with the previously reported axis posteriorizing activity of this protease (Hou et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mRNA overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: HtrA1 overexpression caused a reduction of dorsal fin tissue and fewer melanocytes.
source: HtrA1 overexpression also caused a reduction of dorsal fin tissue (open arrowheads) and fewer melanocytes (arrow), suggesting that HtrA1 inhibits the formation of NC-derived structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mRNA overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: HtrA1 inhibits the formation of NC-derived structures.
source: HtrA1 overexpression also caused a reduction of dorsal fin tissue (open arrowheads) and fewer melanocytes (arrow), suggesting that HtrA1 inhibits the formation of NC-derived structures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduction of NC-derived structures upon HtrA1 overexpression.

claim: A single dorsal injection of HtrA1 mRNA did not affect the expression of cranial and trunk NC markers at stage 18.
source: A single dorsal injection of HtrA1 mRNA did not affect the expression of cranial and trunk NC markers at stage 18 (Figure 3E and F) but blocked EMT and migration of NC cells at stages 20 and 26 (Figure 3H–K and Figure 6B–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3.

claim: A single dorsal injection of HtrA1 mRNA blocked EMT and migration of NC cells at stages 20 and 26.
source: A single dorsal injection of HtrA1 mRNA did not affect the expression of cranial and trunk NC markers at stage 18 (Figure 3E and F) but blocked EMT and migration of NC cells at stages 20 and 26 (Figure 3H–K and Figure 6B–C').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mRNA overexpression experiments shown in Figure 3 and Figure 6.

claim: HtrA1 overexpression caused migratory defects in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Quantitative analysis showed that HtrA1 overexpression caused migratory defects in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ventral mRNA injection of HtrA1-derived constructs was less effective in inhibiting the migration of NC cells.
source: Ventral mRNA injection of HtrA1-derived constructs does not properly target the NC and therefore was less effective in inhibiting the migration of this cell population (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dorsal injection of HtrA1-MO failed to affect the induction of the NC marker Twist.
source: Dorsal injection of HtrA1-MO failed both to affect the induction of the NC marker Twist (Figure 3G) and to alter the migration of Twist+ cells (Figure 3L), suggesting that knockdown of HtrA1 appears not to affect NC development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dorsal injection of HtrA1-MO failed to alter the migration of Twist+ cells.
source: Dorsal injection of HtrA1-MO failed both to affect the induction of the NC marker Twist (Figure 3G) and to alter the migration of Twist+ cells (Figure 3L), suggesting that knockdown of HtrA1 appears not to affect NC development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Knockdown of HtrA1 appears not to affect NC development.
source: Dorsal injection of HtrA1-MO failed both to affect the induction of the NC marker Twist (Figure 3G) and to alter the migration of Twist+ cells (Figure 3L), suggesting that knockdown of HtrA1 appears not to affect NC development.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing no effect of HtrA1 knockdown on NC development.

claim: Upregulation of HtrA1 protease activity inhibits the migration but not the specification of NC cells.
source: We conclude that upregulation of HtrA1 protease activity inhibits the migration but not the specification of NC cells.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results.

claim: Cranial NC cells contribute to the craniofacial skeleton.
source: Cranial NC cells contribute to the craniofacial skeleton (Sadaghiani and Thiébaud, 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The mandibular crest stream gives rise to the ethmoid-traberculum (upper jaw), palatoquadrate and Meckel's cartilage (lower jaw).
source: The mandibular crest stream gives rise to the ethmoid-traberculum (upper jaw), palatoquadrate and Meckel's cartilage (lower jaw); the hyoid crest stream supplies the ceratohyal cartilage; and the branchial crest streams form the paired ceratobranchial cartilages (gills) (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and illustrated in Figure 4L.

claim: The hyoid crest stream supplies the ceratohyal cartilage.
source: The mandibular crest stream gives rise to the ethmoid-traberculum (upper jaw), palatoquadrate and Meckel's cartilage (lower jaw); the hyoid crest stream supplies the ceratohyal cartilage; and the branchial crest streams form the paired ceratobranchial cartilages (gills) (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and illustrated in Figure 4L.

claim: The branchial crest streams form the paired ceratobranchial cartilages (gills).
source: The mandibular crest stream gives rise to the ethmoid-traberculum (upper jaw), palatoquadrate and Meckel's cartilage (lower jaw); the hyoid crest stream supplies the ceratohyal cartilage; and the branchial crest streams form the paired ceratobranchial cartilages (gills) (Figure 4L).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge and illustrated in Figure 4L.

claim: Sox9 is a master regulator of chondrogenesis that mediates the condensation of chondrogenic mesenchyme and chondrocyte differentiation.
source: The transcription factor Sox9 is a master regulator of chondrogenesis that mediates the condensation of chondrogenic mesenchyme and chondrocyte differentiation (Suzuki et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: In early tadpoles at stages 40/41, Sox9 expression demarcates chondrogenic precursors in the head mesenchyme.
source: In early tadpoles at stages 40/41, Sox9 expression demarcates chondrogenic precursors in the head mesenchyme (Figure 4A and A').
evidence: This claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Upon microinjection of HtrA1 mRNA into the animal pole of all blastomeres at the four-cell stage, Sox9 expression was reduced in developing cartilage structures.
source: Upon microinjection of HtrA1 mRNA into the animal pole of all blastomeres at the four-cell stage, Sox9 expression was reduced in developing cartilage structures (Figure 4B and B').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mRNA overexpression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: A similar reduction of Sox9+ cartilaginous elements was induced by SerpinE2-MO.
source: A similar reduction of Sox9+ cartilaginous elements was induced by SerpinE2-MO, whereas the control-MO had no effect (Figure 4C–D').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from morpholino knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The control-MO had no effect on Sox9+ cartilaginous elements.
source: A similar reduction of Sox9+ cartilaginous elements was induced by SerpinE2-MO, whereas the control-MO had no effect (Figure 4C–D').
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from control experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: HtrA1 overexpression and SerpinE2 knockdown impair craniofacial cartilage formation.
source: The results suggest that HtrA1 overexpression and SerpinE2 knockdown impair with craniofacial cartilage formation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduction of cartilage structures.

claim: HtrA1 mRNA injection reduced all cartilage structures and lowered the size of the head skeleton by 21%.
source: HtrA1 mRNA injection reduced all cartilage structures and lowered the size of the head skeleton by 21% (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and quantification shown in Figure 4.

claim: SerpinE2-MO decreased the skeleton size by 22% compared to control-morphant siblings.
source: Similarly, SerpinE2-MO decreased the skeleton size by 22% compared to control-morphant siblings (Figure 4I and J, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B, and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and quantification shown in Figure 4.

claim: The coiling pattern of the gut was not affected upon HtrA1 mRNA injection.
source: The coiling pattern of the gut was not affected upon HtrA1 mRNA injection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, arrowhead) and in SerpinE2-morphant tadpoles (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, arrowhead), ruling out an overall delay of embryonic development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: The coiling pattern of the gut was not affected in SerpinE2-morphant tadpoles.
source: The coiling pattern of the gut was not affected upon HtrA1 mRNA injection (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, arrowhead) and in SerpinE2-morphant tadpoles (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, arrowhead), ruling out an overall delay of embryonic development.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: Co-injection of SerpinE2-MO together with non-targeted Flag-SerpinE2 mRNA rescued craniofacial skeleton development.
source: Co-injection of SerpinE2-MO together with non-targeted Flag-SerpinE2 mRNA rescued craniofacial skeleton development (Figure 4K, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from rescue experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: HtrA1 and SerpinE2 regulate the formation of NC-derived cartilage structures.
source: We conclude that HtrA1 and SerpinE2 regulate the formation of NC-derived cartilage structures.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results.

claim: After 4 hr, cells from uninjected explants spread as a coherent sheet toward one side and thereby doubled the surface area compared to the time of plating.
source: After 4 hr, cells from uninjected explants spread as a coherent sheet toward one side and thereby doubled the surface area compared to the time of plating (Figure 5B–B'' and F, filled arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cranial NC explant migration assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: In explants upon injection with HtrA1 mRNA, little cell migration was observed, contributing to only a 20% increase in surface area within 4 hours.
source: In contrast, little cell migration was observed in explants upon injection with HtrA1 mRNA, contributing to only a 20% increase in surface area within this time frame (Figure 5C–C'' and F, open arrowhead).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from cranial NC explant migration assays shown in Figure 5.

claim: SerpinE2-MO inhibited cell migration, leading to only one-tenth of the increase in total surface area that was observed in control-morphant explants.
